lessons.title: Multiply, divide and raise powers
lessons.summary: Read an index, join or cancel equal factors and recognise when a power repeats a whole group.
lessons.objective: Read an index, join or cancel equal factors and recognise when a power repeats a whole group.
lessons.before: Check that you can recognise the base and the index before applying a rule.
lessons.ideas:
In \(7^3\), the base is 7 and the index is 3. The value is \(7\times7\times7\). A base written by itself has index 1.

\(a^m\times a^n=a^{m+n}\) whenever the powers are defined. Keep the common base.

\(\dfrac{a^m}{a^n}=a^{m-n}\) when \(a\ne0\). Start with the numerator index.

\((a^m)^n=a^{mn}\). There are \(n\) groups and each group contains \(m\) equal factors when both indices are positive integers.
lessons.method:
What does an index count?

When rewriting a repeated product, count the copies of the number. The multiplication signs separate the copies.

When do I add the indices?

Read the first group and the second group. Add their counts of equal factors. Write the original base with this new index.

Which index do I subtract?

Count the denominator factors being removed. Subtract this number from the numerator index. Read the result as a power of the original base.

When do I multiply the indices?

Find the size of one group and the number of groups. Their product gives the new index.
mistakes: \(7^3\) asks for three factors of 7. Multiplying \(7\) by \(3\) gives a different value.
Check both the operation and the bases. Adding powers or multiplying powers with different bases does not give this rule.
The numerator and denominator are ordered. Reversing the subtraction usually produces the reciprocal of the correct result.
Two powers next to a multiplication sign use the product rule. A power outside a bracket uses the power-of-a-power rule.

examples.title: Read repeated factors
examples.question: Write \(4\times 4\times 4\) as a single power of \(4\).
examples.solution:
The same number, \(4\), is a factor 3 times. The base is \(4\).

The index records the number of copies. The expression is \(4^{3}\).

examples.title: Multiply powers with the same base
examples.question: Write \(5^{4}\times 5^{7}\) as a single power of \(5\).
examples.solution:
\(5^{4}\) contains 4 copies of the base as factors. \(5^{7}\) adds 7 copies of the same base.

Join the two groups and keep the base: \(5^{4+7}=5^{11}\).

examples.title: Cancel equal factors in a quotient
examples.question: Write \(\frac{4^{9}}{4^{4}}\) as a single power of \(4\).
examples.solution:
Cancel 4 copies of \(4\) from the numerator with the 4 copies in the denominator.

The rest are in the numerator. Use \(4^{9-4}=4^{5}\).

examples.title: Raise a power to another power
examples.question: Write \((7^{3})^{3}\) as a single power of \(7\).
examples.solution:
The outer index creates 3 groups. Each group contains 3 factors of \(7\).

There are \(3\times3=9\) factors of the original base. Write \(7^{9}\).

lessons.title: Zero and negative indices
lessons.summary: Use cancellation to explain the zero index, take reciprocals for negative indices and read signs with brackets.
lessons.objective: Use cancellation to explain the zero index, take reciprocals for negative indices and read signs with brackets.
lessons.before: Check that you can recognise the base and the index before applying a rule.
lessons.ideas:
\(a^0=1\) for \(a\ne0\). Division by zero would not give the argument, so this rule does not define \(0^0\).

\(a^{-n}=\dfrac{1}{a^n}\) for \(a\ne0\). If \(a\) is positive, its reciprocal and its powers stay positive.

For non-zero \(a,b\), \(\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{-n}=\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)^n\). In \((-a)^{-2}\) the negative base is squared before its reciprocal is taken.
lessons.method:
Why does a zero index give one?

To check the value, write a same-base quotient with equal numerator and denominator indices. Compare the value of the quotient with the result of the index rule.

How does a negative index change the value?

Write the reciprocal of the positive-index power. Evaluate that power exactly, then reduce the fraction if you can.

What belongs to the base?

Identify the bracketed base before doing the calculation. For a negative index on a fraction, turn over the entire base fraction and then apply the positive index.
mistakes: Zero names the index. It does not describe the value of a non-zero base raised to that index.
The minus sign on an index asks for a reciprocal. It does not change a positive value into a negative value.
In \(-5^{-2}\), the power applies to 5 first and the leading minus gives \(-\dfrac1{25}\). In \((-5)^{-2}\) the sign is within the base.

examples.title: Use the zero-index rule
examples.question: Work out the exact value of \(9^{0}\).
examples.solution:
The fraction \(\frac{9^{4}}{9^{4}}\) compares the same non-zero value with itself. Its value is 1.

The index rule gives \(9^{4-4}=9^{0}\). It follows that \(9^{0}=1\).

examples.title: Evaluate a negative integer index
examples.question: Work out the exact value of \(3^{-4}\).
examples.solution:
The negative index means take the reciprocal. Write \(3^{-4}=\frac{1}{3^{4}}\).

Evaluate the positive-index power below the fraction bar. The answer is \(\frac{1}{81}\).

examples.title: Use a negative index on a fraction
examples.question: Work out the exact value of \(\left(\frac{6}{7}\right)^{-2}\).
examples.solution:
Find the reciprocal of the whole fraction, \(\frac{7}{6}\). The index is now \(2\).

Raise both parts of the reciprocal to that power. The result is \(\frac{49}{36}\).

lessons.title: Combine integer indices
lessons.summary: Put several index rules in order, rewrite a numerical base to match another and keep addition separate from multiplication.
lessons.objective: Put several index rules in order, rewrite a numerical base to match another and keep addition separate from multiplication.
lessons.before: Check that you can recognise the base and the index before applying a rule.
lessons.ideas:
For example, \(\dfrac{6^2}{6^{-3}}=6^{2-(-3)}=6^5\). Subtracting a negative index increases the resulting index.

In \(\dfrac{a^p\times a^q}{a^r}\), the numerator helps form \(p+q\). The denominator then changes the index to \(p+q-r\).

For \(36^3\) and \(6^4\), first use \(36=6^2\). The first power becomes \((6^2)^3=6^6\).

\((ab)^n=a^nb^n\) for the numerical powers used here. By contrast, \(a^m+a^n\) does not combine by adding indices.
lessons.method:
How do I subtract a negative index?

Put brackets around signed indices. Subtract the denominator index from the numerator index. Simplify the signed calculation before deciding if a reciprocal is needed.

Which rule comes first?

Write a line for the numerator operation. Then subtract the denominator index. If you are asked to evaluate, turn a final negative index into a reciprocal.

Can I rewrite the bases to match?

Rewrite the larger base inside brackets. Multiply its inner and outer indices. Now compare the two same-base powers and choose the appropriate operation.

What if I see addition or a product in brackets?

If the whole base is a product, give each factor the outer index. If two powers are added, evaluate separately or factorise a common factor.
mistakes: Changing the index of a denominator power may change the value of a quotient. Keep the denominator’s minus sign until you have written the subtraction.
Add the numerator’s signed indices. Treat a negative numerator index as a signed addend, not as a signal to flip the whole quotient.
Indices refer to their own bases. Do not subtract two indices until you have found equal bases in a quotient.
The power rule for a product does not distribute across addition. Keep the original operation visible at each step.

examples.title: Subtract a signed index
examples.question: Write \(\frac{7^{-4}}{7^{-3}}\) as a single power of \(7\).
examples.solution:
The powers have the same base. Use numerator index minus denominator index.

The index is \((-4)-(-3)=-1\). The single power is \(7^{-1}\).

examples.title: Combine multiplication and division
examples.question: Write \(\frac{6^{6}\times 6^{-1}}{6^{6}}\) as a single power of \(6\).
examples.solution:
The numerator is a product. Its index is \(6+(-1)=5\).

Subtract the denominator index. The result is \(6^{-1}\).

examples.title: Rewrite one base to match the other
examples.question: Write \(\frac{27^{2}}{3^{4}}\) as a single power of \(3\).
examples.solution:
Rewrite \(27\) as \(3^{3}\). Raising this to index \(2\) gives \(3^{6}\).

Now the bases match. Divide by subtracting \(4\) from the numerator index, giving \(3^{2}\).

examples.title: Recognise when the product rule does not apply
examples.question: Work out the exact value of \(3^{2}+3^{1}\).
examples.solution:
The two powers are added. The same-base multiplication rule does not apply to this operation.

Evaluate each power, then add: \(9+3=12\).

lessons.title: Fractional indices (Extended)
lessons.summary: Read the root and power in a fractional index and find exact values for positive numerical bases.
lessons.objective: Read the root and power in a fractional index and find exact values for positive numerical bases.
lessons.before: Check that you can recognise the base and the index before applying a rule.
lessons.ideas:
\(a^{\frac{1}{n}}=\sqrt[n]{a}\) for \(a>0\). Squaring the square root or cubing the cube root takes you back to the base.

\(a^{\frac{m}{n}}=(\sqrt[n]{a})^m\). The denominator gives the root. The numerator gives the power of that root.

\(a^{-\frac{m}{n}}=\dfrac{1}{(\sqrt[n]{a})^m}\) for \(a>0\). Use the reciprocal as the final step.

For positive \(a,b\), \(\sqrt[n]{\dfrac{a}{b}}=\dfrac{\sqrt[n]{a}}{\sqrt[n]{b}}\). The following power then acts on both parts of that fraction.
lessons.method:
What root does the denominator give?

Read the denominator and write the radical. Find the positive value that gives the original base when raised to that denominator.

Which comes first, the root or the power?

Find the root using the denominator. Write that result before raising it to the numerator power. Check that you carried out both steps.

Where does the reciprocal belong?

Work out the root, apply the numerator power, then put the result under 1. If the bases match, the quotient rule also works with fractional indices. For example, \(\dfrac{125^{\frac23}}{125^{-\frac13}}=125^{\frac23-(-\frac13)}=125\).

What if the base is already a fraction?

Take the appropriate root of the numerator and denominator. Raise this fraction to the numerator power of the index. Only take a reciprocal if the original index was negative.
mistakes: The denominator is the root order. It does not tell you to divide the base by that number.
A single root only finishes the calculation when the numerator is 1. If it is larger, you still have a power to apply.
Taking the reciprocal of just the numerator of the exponent changes the question. Keep the root and power together before taking a reciprocal of their value.
Check what the brackets contain before taking a root. Applying the root to just the numerator leaves part of the base unchanged.

examples.title: Read a unit fractional index as a root
examples.question: Work out the exact value of \(343^{\frac{1}{3}}\).
examples.solution:
The denominator 3 names the root. Rewrite the expression as \(\sqrt[3]{343}\).

The positive number \(7\) gives \(343\) when raised to the power \(3\). So the root is \(7\).

examples.title: Take a root before raising the power
examples.question: Work out the exact value of \(49^{\frac{3}{2}}\).
examples.solution:
The denominator 2 gives \(\sqrt{49}=7\). Taking the root first keeps the number small.

The numerator 3 says to raise that root to the power \(3\). This gives \(7^{3}=343\).

examples.title: Combine a fractional index and a negative sign
examples.question: Work out the exact value of \(4^{-\frac{3}{2}}\).
examples.solution:
Use the positive index first. The square root of \(4\) is \(2\).

Raise the root to the power \(3\) to get \(8\). The original index was negative, so the answer is the reciprocal \(\frac{1}{8}\).

examples.title: Evaluate a fractional index of a fraction
examples.question: Work out the exact value of \(\left(\frac{125}{729}\right)^{-\frac{2}{3}}\).
examples.solution:
The denominator of the index is 3. Take that root of both the numerator and denominator of the base. The root is \(\frac{5}{9}\).

Raise the root to the power \(2\), giving \(\frac{25}{81}\). Take its reciprocal to get \(\frac{81}{25}\).
